quick.topic: Check your join didn’t multiply rows
quick.summary: Why a query can double revenue, and two checks that catch it.
quick.takeaway: Count rows before and after the join.

parts.title: Check your join didn’t multiply rows

beats.line: My revenue query shows three times finance’s number. Did I break something?
Did you join orders to their items?
Yes, to get the product names.
Then each order appears once per item. Its total counts again each time.
Analysts call this a fan out.
Can I just say the rows multiply?
Check it. Count rows before the join, and after.
Then compare your total with a number you trust.
One thousand orders became three thousand rows. I’ll sum each item’s own price.

quiz.question: After joining orders to order items, revenue comes out three times too high. What is the most likely cause?
options: Each order now appears once per item
quiz.explanation: The join repeats each order row for every item, so the order total is counted several times.

quiz.question: Checking row counts before and after a join helps catch double counting.
quiz.explanation: If rows grow when they should not, the join is multiplying them.
